elements.text:
Overall Merit Statement

The overall merit statement summarizes why your research output - across all or some of your publications, data sets, or research software contributions - made an important substantive contribution to the field. This could include, for example:
  • a consistent research programme across multiple papers
  • a new theory that was developed or tested for the first time
  • a series of experiments that rejected or confirmed a long debated effect
Please focus on the merit of your overarching research program. Later, you will be able to add specific merit statements for individual research outputs.

Do not provide information on societal or scientific impact or information on citation statistics here, but focus on the intrinsic quality of the research output itself - regardless whether it had impact yet or not. Age- and field-normalized citation statistics will be automatically retrieved for each submitted work.

A difficult situation is the distinction between “not applicable” and “not available”. Sometimes authors argue that it is “not possible” to share the data, while data sharing on a restrictive level (Zugriffsklasse 2) actually would be possible. In this case, you have to judge whether it actually was impossible to share (→ “not applicable”). Also sensitive data could be shared if you ask for consent and use a restrictive re-use license. Hence, if they could have shared the data (probably with some effort), choose “not available”.
If the paper cites a data set without an URL (or an invalid URL), and after a reasonable time of searching you could not find the data set, choose “not available”.

elements.tip_external:
To judge whether “Parts” or “Entire” scripts have been shared you need to take a quick look into the scripts themselves.
A typical situation for “parts of scripts” is when the main analyses are provided (e.g., a set of t-tests or a linear regression), but no data preprocessing is shared. • {$P_ReproducibleScripts_FAIR_TimestampedRepository | Timestamped repository: Any repository that records and displays the timestamp when a file has been first uploaded and the last time it has been modified (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, OSF, Zenodo)

• Search for Open License: This license could be stated in ...

elements.title: Correctness of computational results has been independently verified

options.text: Computational reproducibility of MAIN results has been independently verified using the original code
Computational reproducibility of ALL numerical results has been independently verified using the original code

elements.info:
• Independent means that someone who is not a co-author verified the computational reproducibility.

This has rarely been implemented so far, but some journals already do these independent checks, and universities start to provide pre-submission certification of computational reproducibility.

  • {:'WorkflowReproducible' | Workflow reproducibility / code completeness check: Code runs without errors or critical warnings on another machine by another person (without comparing the numbers). This is also known as process reproducibility.}
  • {:'MainResultsReproducible' | Computational reproducibility of main results has been independently verified using the original code: Someone compared the figures and main results and asserts a sufficient correspondence with the reported main results.}
  • {:'AllResultsReproducible' | Computational reproducibility of all numerical results has been independently verified using the original code: Someone compared all figures and numbers and asserts a sufficient correspondence with the reported results.}
  • {:'AnalysisReplication' | Analysis replication (independent implementation): Somebody independently implemented the analyses, without looking at the original code, and asserts a sufficient correspondence with the reported main results.}

{:'WorkflowReproducible', 'MainResultsReproducible', 'AllResultsReproducible', 'AnalysisReplication' | The bonus point is only given when a public verification report/certificate with a persistent identifier is available.}
elements.background: 'In the context of mathematics, Stodden et al. distinguish between verification and validation; following their definition, a CODECHECK [or reproducibility check] ensures verification of computational results, i.e., checking that code generates the output it claims to create, but not a validation, i.e., checking that the code implements the right algorithm [or statistical model] to solve the specific research problem.' (see Nüst & Eglen, 2021).

elements.info:
Open Material refers to all material that is necessary to replicate a study. It typically includes questionnaire items, stimuli, texts for vignettes, or code for software that controls the experimental flow. {:'YesParts', 'YesEntire' | Only choose 'Yes' if the material substantially exceeds the open reproducible scripts. }
The main question for this item is: Was there material that could have been uploaded (i.e., without copyright restrictions)?

  • {:'Minimal' | Choose ‘Obviously 'iIncomplete material' if some material could have been uploaded, but no justification for the ommission is given. }
  • {:'NotApplicable' | When to choose 'Not applicable':
    • If no material has been used in the publication, or the entire material is contained in the open reproducible scripts.
    • 'Not applicable' is the default if you chose 'reuse of existing data set', 'meta-analysis' or 'simulation' above; but if there is additional material that shows an own contribution then assign 'Yes, entire material'.

    • If some material has been uploaded (e.g., some additional supplemental results) but the questionnaires not because they were copyrighted, and no other material was ommitted, choose “not applicable” in favor of the applicant.
    }

The pure existence of an Electronic Supplemental Material does not necessarily count as Open Material, for example if it only contains additional analyses or tables.

• Is a link to open materials provided (don't forget to check Appendix and Supplemental Materials)
  • Expect 'entire material' as default if materials are available (only if the material is obviously not complete and no reasonable explanation is given, assign 'parts of materials')

options.text: Yes (but not RR) [provide doi or URL]

elements.info:
{:'Yes' | Only choose 'Yes' if the preregistration is time-stamped/registered before the publication of the study (check date). Typical preregistration platforms include: OSF, aspredicted.org, ZPID Prereg, ClinicalTrials.gov/.org, Euclinicaltrials.eu, Clinicaltrialsregister.eu, DRKS.}

Multi Study Paper Case: Only choose 'Yes' if your nominated study has been preregistered.

When to choose 'No'
  • If the study was not preregistered or if preregistration is not time-stamped/registered

When to choose 'Not applicable':
  • If the study type is 'Simulation' (except from benchmarking experiments), 'mainly theoretical Review' or no data has been used in a substantive way.
    • In rare cases: When the theory arguably is so precise that no preregistration is necessary.
  • There also might be other cases with reasonable justifications for no preregistration.
elements.tip_external:
• It only counts if a link to the preregistration is provided.
  • Search words: preregist*, pre-regist*, regist*, aspredicted, OSF. For clinical trials: Prospero, ClinicalTrials

elements.title: ⤷ DOI or URL of the preregistration
⤷ What has been preregistered? (check all that apply)

options.text: Sample size planning (typically: an a priori power analysis; or post-hoc power analysis in case of reused data)
Hypotheses are clearly and explicitly stated.
Inferential criteria (e.g., defining your alpha level)

elements.info:
Sample size: Typically, an a priori power analysis was conducted and is reported. Not enough to receive points:
  • 'We will collect as many participants as possible'
  • Only saying which sample size is aimed at without any rationale. Be careful: The AsPredicted template states 'No need to justify decision'. This would not be sufficient in RESQUE.
If 'reuse of existing data set': Here we expect a post-hoc power analysis that investigates whether the sample size of the reused data set is large enough to test the hypothesized effects with sufficient power.

Hypothesis

Hypotheses in the preregistration should be the same as reported in the paper. Deviations must be explained.
. (External raters: See note below).
A generally formulated research question (“Is there a difference between control and experimental group?”) is not sufficient for a hypothesis. Also if a section states “This study aims to… (e.g., identify effect moderators”, these a general explorative goals, but no hypotheses.
A proper hypothesis should state: (a) the outcome variable (what is the primary outcome?), (b) the predictor variable or intervention, and (c) the direction (or explicitly say “undirected test”).

Operationalizations

  • If you would be able to rebuild the experimental setup based on the preregistered description of the measurement instruments, then assign 'yes'. If it is too vague (e.g. only 'we will use reaction times'), then assign 'no'.
  • If it is ambiguous ('I will use either questionnaire A or B') - without a decision rule - it is 'no'.
  • In a secondary data preregistration ('reuse of existing data set'), the primary outcome should be defined


Analysis Plan

Required to receive point: For each confirmatory hypothesis, there must be …
  • … a specification of the dependent and independent variables with their concrete operationalizations (i.e., what’s the primary outcome?)
  • … a specification of the statistical test (e.g., 'a t-test')


Inferential criteria (e.g., defining your alpha level)
Specified decision rule: E.g., what's the alpha-level? When does a result speak in favor of the hypothesis, when against? (especially when multiple testing was conducted)

## 9. Ihre Rechte (DSGVO)

Sie können Auskunft darüber verlangen,

A) Beim Laden der Seite (technisch erforderlich)

Es erfolgt keine Übertragung an einen Server.

Sie können Ihre Ergebnisse als lokale JSON-Datei exportieren und später wieder importieren. Dabei gilt ebenfalls, dass diese Daten ausschließlich auf Ihrem Gerät gespeichert werden und an keine Server übertragen werden, weder an die LMU noch an Dritte.

  • DOI

9. Ihre Rechte (DSGVO)

Wenn personenbezogene Daten verarbeitet werden, stehen Ihnen im Rahmen der gesetzlichen Voraussetzungen folgende Rechte zu.

Auskunft (Art. 15 DSGVO)

Sie können Auskunft darüber verlangen,

  • ob personenbezogene Daten von Ihnen verarbeitet werden
  • welche Daten verarbeitet werden
  • weitere Informationen zur Verarbeitung

Das Auskunftsrecht kann in bestimmten Fällen eingeschränkt sein (z. B. Art. 10 BayDSG).

Berichtigung (Art. 16 DSGVO)

Sie können die Berichtigung unrichtiger personenbezogener Daten verlangen.

Löschung oder Einschränkung der Verarbeitung (Art. 17 und 18 DSGVO)

Sie können die Löschung oder Einschränkung der Verarbeitung verlangen, sofern die gesetzlichen Voraussetzungen vorliegen.

Das Recht auf Löschung kann eingeschränkt sein, wenn die Verarbeitung zur Wahrnehmung einer Aufgabe im öffentlichen Interesse erforderlich ist (Art. 17 Abs. 3 lit. b DSGVO).

Datenübertragbarkeit (Art. 20 DSGVO)

Sie können verlangen, dass von Ihnen bereitgestellte Daten

  • in einem standardisierten elektronischen Format bereitgestellt werden oder
  • an eine von Ihnen benannte Stelle übermittelt werden.

Voraussetzung ist eine Verarbeitung auf Grundlage einer Einwilligung oder eines Vertrags sowie automatisierte Verarbeitung.

Widerspruch (Art. 21 DSGVO)

Wenn die Verarbeitung zur Wahrnehmung einer öffentlichen Aufgabe erfolgt (Art. 6 Abs. 1 lit. e DSGVO), können Sie aus Gründen Ihrer besonderen Situation jederzeit Widerspruch einlegen.

Widerruf einer Einwilligung

Eine erteilte Einwilligung kann jederzeit mit Wirkung für die Zukunft widerrufen werden.

Title: Etzler et al. (2023): Machine Learning and Risk Assessment: Random Forest Does Not Outperform Logistic Regression in the Prediction of Sexual Recidivism
Abstract: <jats:p> Although many studies supported the use of actuarial risk assessment instruments (ARAIs) because they outperformed unstructured judgments, it remains an ongoing challenge to seek potentials for improvement of their predictive performance. Machine learning (ML) algorithms, like random forests, are able to detect patterns in data useful for prediction purposes without explicitly programming them (e.g., by considering nonlinear effects between risk factors and the criterion). Therefore, the current study aims to compare conventional logistic regression analyses with the random forest algorithm on a sample of N = 511 adult male individuals convicted of sexual offenses. Data were collected at the Federal Evaluation Center for Violent and Sexual Offenders in Austria within a prospective-longitudinal research design and participants were followed-up for an average of M = 8.2 years. The Static-99, containing static risk factors, and the Stable-2007, containing stable dynamic risk factors, were included as predictors. The results demonstrated no superior predictive performance of the random forest compared with logistic regression; furthermore, methods of interpretable ML did not point to any robust nonlinear effects. Altogether, results supported the statistical use of logistic regression for the development and clinical application of ARAIs. </jats:p>

Title: Nosek et al. (2022): Replicability, Robustness, and Reproducibility in Psychological Science
P_OpenMaterials_NAExplanation: No material was used, other than the data itself.
Abstract: <jats:p>Replication—an important, uncommon, and misunderstood practice—is gaining appreciation in psychology. Achieving replicability is important for making research progress. If findings are not replicable, then prediction and theory development are stifled. If findings are replicable, then interrogation of their meaning and validity can advance knowledge. Assessing replicability can be productive for generating and testing hypotheses by actively confronting current understandings to identify weaknesses and spur innovation. For psychology, the 2010s might be characterized as a decade of active confrontation. Systematic and multi-site replication projects assessed current understandings and observed surprising failures to replicate many published findings. Replication efforts highlighted sociocultural challenges such as disincentives to conduct replications and a tendency to frame replication as a personal attack rather than a healthy scientific practice, and they raised awareness that replication contributes to self-correction. Nevertheless, innovation in doing and understanding replication and its cousins, reproducibility and robustness, has positioned psychology to improve research practices and accelerate progress.</jats:p>

Woll & Schönbrodt (2020): A Series of Meta-Analytic Tests of the Efficacy of Long-Term Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy
Abstract: <jats:p>Abstract. Recent meta-analyses come to conflicting conclusions about the efficacy of long-term psychoanalytic psychotherapy (LTPP). Our first goal was to reproduce the most recent meta-analysis by Leichsenring, Abbass, Luyten, Hilsenroth, and Rabung (2013) who found evidence for the efficacy of LTPP in the treatment of complex mental disorders. Our replicated effect sizes were in general slightly smaller. Second, we conducted an updated meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing LTPP (lasting for at least 1 year and 40 sessions) to other forms of psychotherapy in the treatment of complex mental disorders. We focused on a transparent research process according to open science standards and applied a series of elaborated meta-analytic procedures to test and control for publication bias. Our updated meta-analysis comprising 191 effect sizes from 14 eligible studies revealed small, statistically significant effect sizes at post-treatment for the outcome domains psychiatric symptoms, target problems, social functioning, and overall effectiveness (Hedges’ g ranging between 0.24 and 0.35). The effect size for the domain personality functioning (0.24) was not significant ( p = .08). No signs for publication bias could be detected. In light of a heterogeneous study set and some methodological shortcomings in the primary studies, these results should be interpreted cautiously. In conclusion, LTPP might be superior to other forms of psychotherapy in the treatment of complex mental disorders. Notably, our effect sizes represent the additional gain of LTPP versus other forms of primarily long-term psychotherapy. In this case, large differences in effect sizes are not to be expected.</jats:p>

Title: Carter et al. (2019): Correcting for Bias in Psychology: A Comparison of Meta-Analytic Methods
Abstract: <jats:p>Publication bias and questionable research practices in primary research can lead to badly overestimated effects in meta-analysis. Methodologists have proposed a variety of statistical approaches to correct for such overestimation. However, it is not clear which methods work best for data typically seen in psychology. Here, we present a comprehensive simulation study in which we examined how some of the most promising meta-analytic methods perform on data that might realistically be produced by research in psychology. We simulated several levels of questionable research practices, publication bias, and heterogeneity, and used study sample sizes empirically derived from the literature. Our results clearly indicated that no single meta-analytic method consistently outperformed all the others. Therefore, we recommend that meta-analysts in psychology focus on sensitivity analyses—that is, report on a variety of methods, consider the conditions under which these methods fail (as indicated by simulation studies such as ours), and then report how conclusions might change depending on which conditions are most plausible. Moreover, given the dependence of meta-analytic methods on untestable assumptions, we strongly recommend that researchers in psychology continue their efforts to improve the primary literature and conduct large-scale, preregistered replications. We provide detailed results and simulation code at https://osf.io/rf3ys and interactive figures at http://www.shinyapps.org/apps/metaExplorer/ .</jats:p>

Title: Schönbrodt et al. (2018): Testing Similarity Effects with Dyadic Response Surface Analysis
Abstract: <jats:p>Dyadic similarity effect hypotheses state that the (dis)similarity between dyad members (e.g. the similarity on a personality dimension) is related to a dyadic outcome variable (e.g. the relationship satisfaction of both partners). Typically, these hypotheses have been investigated by using difference scores or other profile similarity indices as predictors of the outcome variables. These approaches, however, have been vigorously criticized for their conceptual and statistical shortcomings. Here, we introduce a statistical method that is based on polynomial regression and addresses most of these shortcomings: dyadic response surface analysis. This model is tailored for similarity effect hypotheses and fully accounts for the dyadic nature of relationship data. Furthermore, we provide a tutorial with an illustrative example and reproducible R and Mplus scripts that should assist substantive researchers in precisely formulating, testing, and interpreting their dyadic similarity effect hypotheses. © 2018 European Association of Personality Psychology</jats:p>

Abstract: <jats:p> Embedded in a theoretically founded process model (termed Dynamics of Motive Satisfaction, ‘DynaMoS’), the present study examined the links between the implicit dispositional communion motive, everyday motivational dynamics, and relationship outcomes in couples. Within–subject processes are proposed to explain between–subject associations of dispositional motives and relationship satisfaction. For an empirical test of the model, data on the dispositional partner–related need for communion and global relationship satisfaction were obtained from 152 individuals in heterosexual relationships. In an extensive experience sampling spanning 2 weeks, a subsample of 130 individuals answered questions about their current motivational states, mood, state relationship satisfaction, and experiences with their partner five times a day. The results were largely consistent with the DynaMoS model: (1) individuals with a strong dispositional implicit communion motive reported more often to be in a communal motivational state; (2) communally motivated individuals were more likely to engage in subsequent instrumental behaviour; and (3) relationship experiences that potentially satisfy communion motivation led to more positive relationship outcomes when individuals were motivated before compared with when they were not. It is discussed how these results and the experience sampling method can foster our understanding of how dispositional characteristics translate into everyday processes and shape relationship outcomes.
